text: The new moon is setting up some excellent tides this weekend, and with northerly winds forecast, water temperatures should continue to climb. The big evening high tides will be ideal for chasing quality whiting up on the flats tight against the mangroves. Fresh yabbies remain hard to beat, so it’s worth getting out early to pump a few on the afternoon low. Beach worms are also proving highly effective and continue to account for plenty of fish. The large afternoon low tides will create plenty of opportunities for flathead anglers, with many of the larger drains becoming accessible as water levels drop. There’s also the chance of encountering threadfin salmon and even the odd barramundi in these areas. Mangrove jacks should be firing on the combination of warm water, larger tides and northerly winds. Soft plastics in the 3-5 inch range worked deep into the snags on the back end of the run-out tide are producing fish. Bream and cod are also active around the same structure. Grunter continue to fish well throughout the creek systems. Prawn-style lures and soft vibes are working nicely, while anglers fishing baits are finding success with strips of squid and mullet. Further afield, reports of school and spotted mackerel have come from around Big Mick and Inskip Point. Traditional trolling methods such as planers rigged with small spoons are working, while small hardbodies in the 80-120mm range are also worth a try.
credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

text: Fishing has been fairly consistent through the Noosa River this week, with bream the standout species throughout the Noosaville reaches and up towards the First Lake. A couple of quality flathead have also been reported around Tewantin and Goat Island, while plenty of smaller flathead in the 35-40cm range are being caught between the river mouth and Woods Bay on the drift. For bait anglers, prawns and worms continue to be the most reliable options and are accounting for most of the catches. Full Report pending. North Reef continues to produce quality snapper, pearl perch, kingfish and Moses perch. With plenty of current pushing across the wider grounds, the closer reefs are proving the more fishable option at present and are holding plenty of fish. Whale numbers remain high offshore, so boaties should continue to keep a careful lookout when travelling to and from the grounds. Flathead continue to feature strongly in the lower estuary, with good numbers of fish being caught throughout the system. A variety of trevally species are also active through Noosa Sound, providing plenty of action for lure and bait anglers alike. There are still a few queenfish around, although getting them to the boat has been a challenge, with sharks proving a persistent nuisance once fish are hooked.
credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

text: Choosing the Right Bait for Fishing Around Rainbow Beach. The right bait around Rainbow Beach depends on where you fish and what you are chasing. Beach worms and pilchards work well for whiting and tailor off the surf, while live prawns and yabbies suit bream and flathead in the estuaries. Gardiner's Tackle World Rainbow Beach , a trusted bait fishing store in the region, stocks fresh and frozen bait for every trip, from the surf to Fraser Island and Double Island Point. Picking the correct bait can make or break a day on the water. Rainbow Beach offers such a wide variety of fishing grounds that a single bait choice rarely covers everything you might encounter. From the open surf beaches to the sheltered creeks of the Cooloola region, each spot calls for a different approach. That's why local anglers rely on a proper bait fishing store rather than guessing at the servo. This guide breaks down the best bait options for the most popular fishing spots around Rainbow Beach, Fraser Island and Double Island Point, so you can walk into your next trip prepared. text: 10 Tips for Mud Crabbing around Rainbow Beach. Catching mud crab in Queensland’s Great Sandy Straits is an exhilarating experience for fishing enthusiasts. Rainbow Beach, strategically located on its southern end offers fishers easy access for both land based and those with their own boat to experience catching the famous QLD “ muddie ”. The pristine waters and diverse mangrove habitats that this beautiful coastal town offers produce some of the tastiest mud crabs in the state. To help you make the most of your mud crabbing adventure, we’ve compiled 10 expert tips that ensure a successful, sustainable, and enjoyable outing. 1. Time Your Trip around the moon phases Timing is everything when it comes to mud crabbing. The best time to go crabbing in Rainbow Beach is the period leading up to the full and new moons. Bigger tides during these periods really get the crabs firing. At this time, crabs are more active and are often visible in the shallow waters, giving you a higher chance of catching them. Keep an eye on tide charts and plan your trip accordingly for maximum success. Although mud crabs are available all year in Rainbow Beach, the peak in numbers occurs from December to March. The best quality (A Grade crab) is caught in the cooler months between April to September 2. text: Wet and windy conditions are expected this weekend, so anglers will be best served heading up the creeks to escape the worst of the showers and south-easterly winds. With the overcast conditions, mangrove jacks should be high on the target list. Surface lures such as frogs and 70-90mm poppers worked tight against snaggy structure are worth a look, while live baits and fresh strips of mullet continue to produce fish. Even when the jacks are quiet, there are usually plenty of cod and bream around to keep rods bending. A few stocked Tin Can Bay barramundi have also been caught over the past couple of weeks as water temperatures continue to rise. Live baits have accounted for some captures, while slowly worked soft plastic prawns remain a reliable option. Crabbing has been a little quiet, although the recent rainfall should help get the crabs moving. It’s still worth setting a few pots, with fresh baits and a longer soak generally producing the best results.
credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

text: Mackerel remain the headline act across the region, with broadbar and school mackerel dominating catches around the Urangan Pier, local beaches and the wider bay. The pier is also producing quality queenfish, giant trevally, golden trevally and the occasional Spanish mackerel, while whiting continue to be caught along the Hervey Bay foreshores and throughout the Great Sandy Straits. The Great Sandy Straits and local river systems are fishing well for grunter, flathead, threadfin salmon, blue salmon and barramundi. Mangrove jacks are firing throughout the western creeks and the Burrum system, while quality whiting are also featuring in the middle reaches. Offshore, coral trout, grassy sweetlip, cod and Spanish mackerel continue to feature, while billfish activity is building with juvenile black marlin, striped marlin and yellowfin tuna all being reported. Around Rooneys Point and Station Hill, the first consistent run of juvenile black marlin for the season has provided plenty of excitement for gamefishers. Fraser Island’s tailor season remains patchy depending on location and conditions, although quality greenbacks are still being caught through the central sector. Anglers are also finding dart, whiting and the occasional trevally along the surf beaches. Boaties should remain aware of lingering whale traffic and patches of nuisance “snot weed” in parts of Platypus Bay and the central bay.
credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

text: There are still some quality flathead being caught through the lower reaches of the Noosa River, with a number of better fish coming from the deeper channels and drop-offs. Bream and whiting remain the bread-and-butter species throughout the system, providing consistent fishing for both bait and lure anglers. A few tailor have also been taken by land-based anglers in the Noosaville reaches over the past week. Not a huge amount to report over the last week.  The closer offshore reefs were fishing well, with North Reef producing a reliable mix of snapper and sweetlip while further afield, Sunshine Reef was yielding quality pearl perch, while Double Island Point produced hard-fighting amberjack along with plenty of snapper. Plenty of fish being caught with The Hards, Double Island Point and North Reef all producing quality catches. A wide range of reef species are on the chew, making this one of the most productive times of the year to head offshore. With conditions and water temperatures aligning, both this month and next are shaping up as prime months for reef fishing, with anglers finding quality fish across both the close and wider grounds. The lower estuary continues to produce some quality flathead, while a number of belter bream have also been reported throughout the system. A few smaller mulloway are being caught in the ski run areas, with soft plastic frog-style lures proving effective on the jewies.
